blocks.text: 1. Multi-Hop RAG
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721259-871511586.png

Recursive RAG closed by pointing toward chasing a chain of dependent facts. Multi-Hop RAG, which chases a chain of dependent facts across several retrieval steps, is that specific chaining pattern named as its own topic.
It lets each hop's retrieved fact determine what the next hop needs to search for, a chained dependency technique explored in full throughout this topic.
2. A Question With A Hidden Dependency Chain
As covered generally in Chain Of Thought's multi-hop questions, a question can name only its final target while the actual answer depends on an unnamed intermediate fact.
That intermediate fact must be found before the final search can even be formed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question type","What retrieval must find first"],"rows":[["Single hop","The answer directly, in one search"],["Multi-hop","An unnamed intermediate fact before the final search"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Hop One Identifies The Missing Link

blocks.alt: Hop One Identifies The Missing Link
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721259-481858023.png
The first hop retrieves whatever fact the question is actually missing to proceed.
This is often an entity name or a specific value the second hop will need.
4. Hop Two Uses The First Hop's Result

blocks.alt: Hop Two Uses The First Hop's Result
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721259-463526586.png
The second hop's search query is built directly from what the first hop just retrieved.
This is a search that could not have been formed before hop one completed.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A second hop query built from the first hop's retrieved entity name could not exist before that first hop completed, since the entity name itself was the unknown the first hop was searching for.

blocks.text: 5. Distinguishing Multi-Hop From Recursive RAG
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721260-298059613.png
Unlike Recursive RAG, which narrows one topic progressively, multi-hop RAG chases a chain of different, dependent facts.
Narrowing and chaining are two distinct refinement patterns.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pattern","What changes across rounds"],"rows":[["Recursive RAG","Same topic, progressively narrower detail"],["Multi-hop RAG","A chain of different, dependent facts"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Identifying How Many Hops Are Needed

blocks.alt: Identifying How Many Hops Are Needed
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721443-891653284.png
Much like classifying query complexity first, as covered in Adaptive RAG, the number of hops needed is not always obvious before starting.
A query decomposition step often estimates the hop count in advance.
7. An Error In An Early Hop Propagates Forward

blocks.alt: An Error In An Early Hop Propagates Forward
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721444-71072427.png
Because each hop depends on the one before it, a wrong intermediate fact corrupts every hop that follows.
This makes early hop accuracy disproportionately important.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A wrong entity name retrieved at hop one sends every following hop searching for the wrong thing, making early hop accuracy far more important than accuracy at the final hop alone.

blocks.text: 8. Cost Scales Linearly With Hop Count
As Advanced RAG covers, each added step costs latency, and every additional hop is its own separate retrieval call.
This is a direct, linear cost increase with the number of hops chased.
9. Recognizing When Multi-Hop RAG Earns Its Per-Hop Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Multi-Hop RAG Earns Its Per-Hop Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721444-527160220.png
Questions with an unnamed intermediate fact require multi-hop retrieval.
A question directly answerable from one document, by contrast, needs only a single hop.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Trying to answer a multi-hop question with a single retrieval call that cannot reach the target.
Confusing multi-hop chaining of different facts with recursive narrowing of one topic.
Underestimating how much an early hop error corrupts every later hop.
Running multi-hop retrieval on a question directly answerable from a single document.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Multi-hop RAG chases a chain of dependent facts across several retrieval steps.
A question can name only its final target while depending on an unnamed intermediate fact.
The first hop retrieves the missing intermediate fact, often an entity name or specific value.
The second hop's search query is built directly from what the first hop just retrieved.
Multi-hop RAG chains different, dependent facts, unlike recursive RAG which narrows one topic.
A query decomposition step often estimates the number of hops needed in advance.
An error in an early hop propagates forward and corrupts every hop that follows.
Every additional hop is its own retrieval call, so cost scales linearly with hop count.
